Is California’s Proposed Billionaire Tax in Trouble? New Polls Find Bad News
Two public nonpartisan surveys show Proposition 40 trailing in the final days of voting. Meanwhile, an initiative to require voter ID in California is losing by double digits.
Oct 29, 2026
Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) speaks at a rally dubbed "Ballots Over Billionaires" at The Novo on Oct. 5, 2026, in Los Angeles, California. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders joined Khanna for the event in support of Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of approximately 200 California billionaires, with most of the revenue intended to offset cuts to Medi-Cal and other healthcare services. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
A proposal to tax California’s billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12106033/the-political-calculus-behind-newsoms-opposition-to-californias-billionaire-tax) to fund healthcare is trailing in two public, nonpartisan polls released this week, surveys that also found strong opposition to a separate ballot measure that would require voters to show identification at the polls.
Proposition 40 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40), which would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the overall wealth of the state’s billionaires, was tracking below the majority needed to pass in polls from both UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California. With days left to vote in the Nov. 3 midterm election, IGS found just 8% of likely voters still undecided on the measure, which billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12104645/sf-billionaire-chris-larsen-on-ai-this-is-an-incredibly-dangerous-moment) have spent more than $300 million to defeat.
Proposition 39 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-39), the voter ID initiative, was also trailing by 20 points in the IGS poll, with just 37% of likely voters saying they were voting yes and 5% undecided. PPIC’s poll found slightly stronger support for the measure, but still had it losing.
Support for Proposition 40 appears to be slipping heading into Election Day. Last month’s PPIC poll had a slim majority in favor before the slide this month.
But in the IGS poll released this week, half of likely voters said they will vote no on Proposition 40, while 42% said they are voting yes. That’s a shift from last month, when the IGS poll found 42% of voters against the measure and 45% backing it.

Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, during the campaign kickoff for the California Billionaire Tax Act at The Wiltern in Los Angeles, on Feb. 18, 2026. Sanders is seeking the support of California voters for a November ballot initiative of an emergency tax on billionaires to help the state’s healthcare system. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
Mark DiCamillo, director of the IGS Poll, said the No on Proposition 40 side is clearly benefiting from the huge amounts of money being poured into defeating the wealth tax.
“A well-funded no side campaign usually has the advantage over yes campaigns, just because all they have to do is raise doubts,” he said.
The poll found Proposition 40 backed by strong majorities of Democrats and voters under 40, and opposed by Republicans and voters over 50. Independents are split.
DiCamillo said the disparity between how younger and older voters view the proposed tax is indicative of a growing split that did not used to exist among the California electorate.

“The generational divide is growing over time, just because the younger set is having a hard time. They can’t afford a house, they can’t reach the American dream,” he said.
“Those are the segments that are now migrating to the Democratic socialists…. They really don’t like the disparity in wealth.”
The fate of the proposed wealth tax will not swing solely on Proposition 40.
Both polls also showed close contests in Propositions 41 and 42, measures put on the ballot by billionaires with language that would nullify the tax if they pass with more votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 41 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-41) would require ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by “special” taxes — those earmarked for a specific purpose. It also would make any new special taxes subject to the state’s existing spending limit. Proposition 42 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-42) would prohibit new taxes on financial assets — such as stocks — and other personal property, and also prohibit most retroactive taxes.
While IGS’s survey showed Propositions 41 and 42 slightly ahead, DiCamillo noted they also found double-digit percentages of likely voters still undecided — and those who have moved since IGS’s September survey have largely turned against the billionaire-backed measures.
“The no side has gained 11 [points] while the yes side is static,” DiCamillo said of Proposition 42.
Proposition 39, the voter ID measure placed on the ballot by Republican lawmakers, has also lost ground since IGS’s poll last month, with the no side gaining 7 percentage points. The survey found Republicans are the only group backing the measure. Likely voters who list no party preference are against it by a 15-point margin in the IGS poll, and majorities of voters in nearly all subgroups — age, race and gender — are opposed.

PPIC found similar opposition: That survey has Proposition 39 down by 17 points, with 58% of likely voters saying they will vote no.
DiCamillo said voters appear to be linking the voter ID measure to President Donald Trump’s push for changes to election laws, which are unpopular with Democrats and independents.
“I think Trump is a factor,” he said. “That really is the winning argument: You go after Trump.”
PPIC also polled on Proposition 45 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-45), the ballot measure written by the California Chamber of Commerce to speed up environmental reviews of construction projects. The survey found likely voters split on the changes to the California Environmental Quality Act, with 46% saying they are voting yes and 50% voting no.
The IGS poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 19-25, and included 2,787 registered voters. The PPIC poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 16-22 and included 1,728 California adult residents.
Both polls have a sampling error of plus or minus 3%.

Is California’s Proposed Billionaire Tax in Trouble? New Polls Find Bad News
Two public nonpartisan surveys show Proposition 40 trailing in the final days of voting. Meanwhile, an initiative to require voter ID in California is losing by double digits.
Oct 29, 2026
Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) speaks at a rally dubbed "Ballots Over Billionaires" at The Novo on Oct. 5, 2026, in Los Angeles, California. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders joined Khanna for the event in support of Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of approximately 200 California billionaires, with most of the revenue intended to offset cuts to Medi-Cal and other healthcare services. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
A proposal to tax California’s billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12106033/the-political-calculus-behind-newsoms-opposition-to-californias-billionaire-tax) to fund healthcare is trailing in two public, nonpartisan polls released this week, surveys that also found strong opposition to a separate ballot measure that would require voters to show identification at the polls.
Proposition 40 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40), which would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the overall wealth of the state’s billionaires, was tracking below the majority needed to pass in polls from both UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California. With days left to vote in the Nov. 3 midterm election, IGS found just 8% of likely voters still undecided on the measure, which billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12104645/sf-billionaire-chris-larsen-on-ai-this-is-an-incredibly-dangerous-moment) have spent more than $300 million to defeat.
Proposition 39 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-39), the voter ID initiative, was also trailing by 20 points in the IGS poll, with just 37% of likely voters saying they were voting yes and 5% undecided. PPIC’s poll found slightly stronger support for the measure, but still had it losing.
Support for Proposition 40 appears to be slipping heading into Election Day. Last month’s PPIC poll had a slim majority in favor before the slide this month.
But in the IGS poll released this week, half of likely voters said they will vote no on Proposition 40, while 42% said they are voting yes. That’s a shift from last month, when the IGS poll found 42% of voters against the measure and 45% backing it.
A T-shirt with a campaign message is seen before the start of a rally led by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, during the campaign kickoff for the California Billionaire Tax Act at The Wiltern in Los Angeles, on Feb. 18, 2026. Sanders is seeking the support of California voters for a November ballot initiative of an emergency tax on billionaires to help the state’s healthcare system. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
Mark DiCamillo, director of the IGS Poll, said the No on Proposition 40 side is clearly benefiting from the huge amounts of money being poured into defeating the wealth tax.
“A well-funded no side campaign usually has the advantage over yes campaigns, just because all they have to do is raise doubts,” he said.
The poll found Proposition 40 backed by strong majorities of Democrats and voters under 40, and opposed by Republicans and voters over 50. Independents are split.
DiCamillo said the disparity between how younger and older voters view the proposed tax is indicative of a growing split that did not used to exist among the California electorate.
From the 2026 Voter Guide
Learn about Proposition 40 and its supporters, opponents, and arguments (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40)
“The generational divide is growing over time, just because the younger set is having a hard time. They can’t afford a house, they can’t reach the American dream,” he said.
“Those are the segments that are now migrating to the Democratic socialists…. They really don’t like the disparity in wealth.”
The fate of the proposed wealth tax will not swing solely on Proposition 40.
Both polls also showed close contests in Propositions 41 and 42, measures put on the ballot by billionaires with language that would nullify the tax if they pass with more votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 41 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-41) would require ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by “special” taxes — those earmarked for a specific purpose. It also would make any new special taxes subject to the state’s existing spending limit. Proposition 42 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-42) would prohibit new taxes on financial assets — such as stocks — and other personal property, and also prohibit most retroactive taxes.
While IGS’s survey showed Propositions 41 and 42 slightly ahead, DiCamillo noted they also found double-digit percentages of likely voters still undecided — and those who have moved since IGS’s September survey have largely turned against the billionaire-backed measures.
“The no side has gained 11 [points] while the yes side is static,” DiCamillo said of Proposition 42.
Proposition 39, the voter ID measure placed on the ballot by Republican lawmakers, has also lost ground since IGS’s poll last month, with the no side gaining 7 percentage points. The survey found Republicans are the only group backing the measure. Likely voters who list no party preference are against it by a 15-point margin in the IGS poll, and majorities of voters in nearly all subgroups — age, race and gender — are opposed.
Sen. Tony Strickland speaks at the Riverside County Registrar of Voters on Monday, March 2, 2026, for a press conference highlighting voter signatures in favor of placing a voter ID measure on the November ballot. (Anjali Sharif-Paul/MediaNews Group/The Sun via Getty Images)
PPIC found similar opposition: That survey has Proposition 39 down by 17 points, with 58% of likely voters saying they will vote no.
DiCamillo said voters appear to be linking the voter ID measure to President Donald Trump’s push for changes to election laws, which are unpopular with Democrats and independents.
“I think Trump is a factor,” he said. “That really is the winning argument: You go after Trump.”
PPIC also polled on Proposition 45 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-45), the ballot measure written by the California Chamber of Commerce to speed up environmental reviews of construction projects. The survey found likely voters split on the changes to the California Environmental Quality Act, with 46% saying they are voting yes and 50% voting no.
The IGS poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 19-25, and included 2,787 registered voters. The PPIC poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 16-22 and included 1,728 California adult residents.
Both polls have a sampling error of plus or minus 3%.

Is California’s Proposed Billionaire Tax in Trouble? New Polls Find Bad News
Two public nonpartisan surveys show Proposition 40 trailing in the final days of voting. Meanwhile, an initiative to require voter ID in California is losing by double digits.
Oct 29, 2026
Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) speaks at a rally dubbed "Ballots Over Billionaires" at The Novo on Oct. 5, 2026, in Los Angeles, California. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders joined Khanna for the event in support of Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of approximately 200 California billionaires, with most of the revenue intended to offset cuts to Medi-Cal and other healthcare services. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
A proposal to tax California’s billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12106033/the-political-calculus-behind-newsoms-opposition-to-californias-billionaire-tax) to fund healthcare is trailing in two public, nonpartisan polls released this week, surveys that also found strong opposition to a separate ballot measure that would require voters to show identification at the polls.
Proposition 40 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40), which would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the overall wealth of the state’s billionaires, was tracking below the majority needed to pass in polls from both UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California. With days left to vote in the Nov. 3 midterm election, IGS found just 8% of likely voters still undecided on the measure, which billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12104645/sf-billionaire-chris-larsen-on-ai-this-is-an-incredibly-dangerous-moment) have spent more than $300 million to defeat.
Proposition 39 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-39), the voter ID initiative, was also trailing by 20 points in the IGS poll, with just 37% of likely voters saying they were voting yes and 5% undecided. PPIC’s poll found slightly stronger support for the measure, but still had it losing.
Support for Proposition 40 appears to be slipping heading into Election Day. Last month’s PPIC poll had a slim majority in favor before the slide this month.
But in the IGS poll released this week, half of likely voters said they will vote no on Proposition 40, while 42% said they are voting yes. That’s a shift from last month, when the IGS poll found 42% of voters against the measure and 45% backing it.
A T-shirt with a campaign message is seen before the start of a rally led by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, during the campaign kickoff for the California Billionaire Tax Act at The Wiltern in Los Angeles, on Feb. 18, 2026. Sanders is seeking the support of California voters for a November ballot initiative of an emergency tax on billionaires to help the state’s healthcare system. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
Mark DiCamillo, director of the IGS Poll, said the No on Proposition 40 side is clearly benefiting from the huge amounts of money being poured into defeating the wealth tax.
“A well-funded no side campaign usually has the advantage over yes campaigns, just because all they have to do is raise doubts,” he said.
The poll found Proposition 40 backed by strong majorities of Democrats and voters under 40, and opposed by Republicans and voters over 50. Independents are split.
DiCamillo said the disparity between how younger and older voters view the proposed tax is indicative of a growing split that did not used to exist among the California electorate.

Learn about Proposition 40 and its supporters, opponents, and arguments (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40)
“The generational divide is growing over time, just because the younger set is having a hard time. They can’t afford a house, they can’t reach the American dream,” he said.
“Those are the segments that are now migrating to the Democratic socialists…. They really don’t like the disparity in wealth.”
The fate of the proposed wealth tax will not swing solely on Proposition 40.
Both polls also showed close contests in Propositions 41 and 42, measures put on the ballot by billionaires with language that would nullify the tax if they pass with more votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 41 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-41) would require ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by “special” taxes — those earmarked for a specific purpose. It also would make any new special taxes subject to the state’s existing spending limit. Proposition 42 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-42) would prohibit new taxes on financial assets — such as stocks — and other personal property, and also prohibit most retroactive taxes.
While IGS’s survey showed Propositions 41 and 42 slightly ahead, DiCamillo noted they also found double-digit percentages of likely voters still undecided — and those who have moved since IGS’s September survey have largely turned against the billionaire-backed measures.
“The no side has gained 11 [points] while the yes side is static,” DiCamillo said of Proposition 42.
Proposition 39, the voter ID measure placed on the ballot by Republican lawmakers, has also lost ground since IGS’s poll last month, with the no side gaining 7 percentage points. The survey found Republicans are the only group backing the measure. Likely voters who list no party preference are against it by a 15-point margin in the IGS poll, and majorities of voters in nearly all subgroups — age, race and gender — are opposed.
Sen. Tony Strickland speaks at the Riverside County Registrar of Voters on Monday, March 2, 2026, for a press conference highlighting voter signatures in favor of placing a voter ID measure on the November ballot. (Anjali Sharif-Paul/MediaNews Group/The Sun via Getty Images)
PPIC found similar opposition: That survey has Proposition 39 down by 17 points, with 58% of likely voters saying they will vote no.
DiCamillo said voters appear to be linking the voter ID measure to President Donald Trump’s push for changes to election laws, which are unpopular with Democrats and independents.
“I think Trump is a factor,” he said. “That really is the winning argument: You go after Trump.”
PPIC also polled on Proposition 45 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-45), the ballot measure written by the California Chamber of Commerce to speed up environmental reviews of construction projects. The survey found likely voters split on the changes to the California Environmental Quality Act, with 46% saying they are voting yes and 50% voting no.
The IGS poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 19-25, and included 2,787 registered voters. The PPIC poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 16-22 and included 1,728 California adult residents.
Both polls have a sampling error of plus or minus 3%.

Proposition 41 would limit the state's ability to enact certain new taxes that exempt revenue from California's constitutional spending limit.
It would also require audits of new special tax proposals before they're placed on the ballot.
A yes vote would establish the proposed restrictions and auditing requirements.
A no vote would leave the existing rules in place.
Supporters say the measure would strengthen fiscal accountability and limit the state's ability to avoid constitutional spending restrictions.
Critics argue that the proposal could restrict future state revenue options and interfere with other tax measures, including the proposed billionaire wealth tax under Proposition 40.

### What will the measure do?
Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot.
The auditor would examine whether the program is achieving its goals, how to cut the program’s costs by at least 10% annually and other areas.
Under the act, new or higher special taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, would be audited every four years.
The act also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.
That could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.

## How the Limits Work for Other Entities
#### School and Community College Districts
The state has two ways to allow districts to spend above their limits.
Either the state transfers some of its own limit to districts or it absorbs some of the district’s excess appropriations and counts those at the state level.
Either mechanism allows the districts to spend above their limits and reduce the state’s room.

## Rainy day fund deposits would stop counting toward the state appropriations limit under Proposition 2:
The state appropriations limit, adopted by voters in 1979 and often called the Gann limit after its sponsor Paul Gann, caps how much tax revenue the state can spend each year.
Its purpose, as the Senate Budget Committee describes it, is to keep inflation-adjusted spending per person under 1978–79 levels.
Money put into reserves counts against the limit in the year it is deposited, just as spending does.
...
Prop 2 changes when savings count.
Deposits into the rainy day fund would not count against the limit when they are made.
They would count in the year the money is withdrawn and spent.
The measure gives the same treatment to the state's temporary surplus holding account, a statutory account where the state parks revenue that may not last, up to 10% of General Fund taxes in a year.
The state put $6.4 billion into that account for 2026–27, according to the LAO's overview of the budget, which says neither it nor the Department of Finance treats the account as a reserve.
The practical effect is that in a boom year, when the state is most likely to be near the limit, saving would no longer use up room under it.
The Budget Center estimates the change could add up to a few billion dollars of room in some years.

#### School and Community College Districts
The state has two ways to allow districts to spend above their limits.
Either the state transfers some of its own limit to districts or it absorbs some of the district’s excess appropriations and counts those at the state level.
Either mechanism allows the districts to spend above their limits and reduce the state’s room.
Currently, there is about $17 billion in district revenues above their limits that is counted at the state level.
***Some Districts Have Room Under Their Limits.*** Although most districts have proceeds of taxes in excess of their local limits, about 10 percent of districts are below their limits.
We refer to this difference between the limit and appropriations subject to the limit as “room.”
This situation can occur if a district had a historically high appropriations limit, or if a district has been experiencing relatively slow growth in funding.

content.text:
I won't give a one-word verdict on this one. Whether Prop. 41 is a good idea depends mostly on how you view the billionaire tax (Prop. 40) and how you weigh audit transparency against spending-cap flexibility. That's a value judgment, so I'll lay out the evidence and let you decide.

**What it does**
- Requires a State Auditor review of programs funded by any citizen-proposed special tax once backers reach 25% of the needed signatures. The summary goes in the voter guide and must recommend ways to cut program costs by at least 10% a year. Approved special taxes get audits every four years.
- Bars new state taxes enacted or taking effect after Jan. 1, 2026 from being exempt from the 1979 Gann spending limit.
- If it gets more yes votes than Prop. 40 and both pass, it can nullify Prop. 40, though courts would resolve the conflict.
- The LAO says the net fiscal effect is unknown. Audit costs are likely in the low millions per year.

**Strongest case for yes**
- Voters get independent performance information before approving special taxes, plus ongoing reviews. Even the Mercury News board wrote that the audit idea "could be valuable."
- Supporters say new taxes shouldn't escape a voter-approved cap, and that the 10% item is a recommendation, not a mandate.
- Backers include CalCPAs, CalTax, the CalChamber, the California Republican Party, and the San Diego Union-Tribune and OC Register.

**Strongest case for no**
- The spending-cap provision is broad and permanent. The League of Women Voters, SPUR, the SF Chronicle, the Sacramento Bee, and the Mercury News/East Bay Times all oppose it, citing future revenue flexibility.
- A law-professor memo warns it could reach existing Medi-Cal financing (the MCO tax and hospital fee) and Prop. 3. Its authors partly drafted Prop. 40, and the state would likely contest those readings.
- Critics say the audits duplicate the State Auditor's and LAO's existing work and that the 10% target is arbitrary. The campaign is funded largely by Google co-founder Sergey Brin's group, and opponents call it a poison pill.
- The cap isn't binding now. The LAO projects about $27 billion of room in 2026–27, so the main risk is future budgets.

**How Prop. 40 changes the math**
- If you want the billionaire tax to take effect, vote no on 41. A yes that outpolls Prop. 40 could void it.
- If you want Prop. 40 to fail, a no on 40 does that by itself. A yes on 41 would then add its audit and spending-cap rules, which take effect if it passes.

I couldn't find election results, so this is pre-election information. The latest polls have 41 short of a majority: PPIC had 48% yes and 49% no (Oct. 16–22), and Berkeley IGS had 38% yes, 47% no, and 16% undecided (Oct. 19–25).

If you tell me where you stand on Prop. 40 or which trade-off matters most to you, I can help you work through the rest.

I won't give a one-word verdict on this one. Whether Prop. 41 is a good idea depends mostly on how you view the billionaire tax (Prop. 40) and how you weigh audit transparency against spending-cap flexibility. That's a value judgment, so I'll lay out the evidence and let you decide.

**What it does**
- Requires a State Auditor review of programs funded by any citizen-proposed special tax once backers reach 25% of the needed signatures. The summary goes in the voter guide and must recommend ways to cut program costs by at least 10% a year. Approved special taxes get audits every four years.
- Bars new state taxes enacted or taking effect after Jan. 1, 2026 from being exempt from the 1979 Gann spending limit.
- If it gets more yes votes than Prop. 40 and both pass, it can nullify Prop. 40, though courts would resolve the conflict.
- The LAO says the net fiscal effect is unknown. Audit costs are likely in the low millions per year.

**Strongest case for yes**
- Voters get independent performance information before approving special taxes, plus ongoing reviews. Even the Mercury News board wrote that the audit idea "could be valuable."
- Supporters say new taxes shouldn't escape a voter-approved cap, and that the 10% item is a recommendation, not a mandate.
- Backers include CalCPAs, CalTax, the CalChamber, the California Republican Party, and the San Diego Union-Tribune and OC Register.

**Strongest case for no**
- The spending-cap provision is broad and permanent. The League of Women Voters, SPUR, the SF Chronicle, the Sacramento Bee, and the Mercury News/East Bay Times all oppose it, citing future revenue flexibility.
- A law-professor memo warns it could reach existing Medi-Cal financing (the MCO tax and hospital fee) and Prop. 3. Its authors partly drafted Prop. 40, and the state would likely contest those readings.
- Critics say the audits duplicate the State Auditor's and LAO's existing work and that the 10% target is arbitrary. The campaign is funded largely by Google co-founder Sergey Brin's group, and opponents call it a poison pill.
- The cap isn't binding now. The LAO projects about $27 billion of room in 2026–27, so the main risk is future budgets.

**How Prop. 40 changes the math**
- If you want the billionaire tax to take effect, vote no on 41. A yes that outpolls Prop. 40 could void it.
- If you want Prop. 40 to fail, a no on 40 does that by itself. A yes on 41 would then add its audit and spending-cap rules, which take effect if it passes.

I couldn't find election results, so this is pre-election information. The latest polls have 41 short of a majority: PPIC had 48% yes and 49% no (Oct. 16–22), and Berkeley IGS had 38% yes, 47% no, and 16% undecided (Oct. 19–25).

If you tell me where you stand on Prop. 40 or which trade-off matters most to you, I can help you work through the rest.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. The Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide (VIG).
Voter Initiative Process. California citizens may propose state laws and constitutional amendments through the statewide initiative process. Supporters of an initiative collect signatures from registered voters to qualify their initiative for the ballot. State law sets how many valid signatures supporters must collect to qualify their initiative for the ballot. Supporters notify the Secretary of State once they have gathered 25 percent of the necessary signatures.
Special Taxes. State taxes can be raised by the Legislature or by voters. When a “special tax” is created, the revenue from that tax is dedicated to a specific purpose or program. For example, certain fuel taxes can only be used to pay for public roads and other transportation programs.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments follow the law, use money, and run their programs. These reviews are called audits. An audit may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly over time while other audits are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter Initiative Process. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would receive funds from a new or increased special tax proposed through the voter initiative process. This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a measure for the ballot, which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the ballot. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor would include in these audits, including identifying ways to reduce an audited program’s annual costs by 10 percent. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to write a summary of each audit. If a proposed voter initiative with a special tax qualifies for the ballot, Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor’s summary to be included in the VIG. If voters approve the special tax, the cost of the one-time audit would be paid from the new tax revenues.
Ongoing Audits of Programs Receiving Funds From New or Increased Special Taxes. Proposition 41 also requires the State Auditor to periodically review programs that receive funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or by voters after January 1, 2026. These ongoing audits would happen every four years. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor will include in these audits, including recommendations to improve program efficiency. Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of this ongoing work will be paid using the new tax revenue.
State Appropriations Limit. The State Constitution limits how much tax revenues the state can spend each year. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes and special taxes. However, certain types of spending, for example for infrastructure, are excluded from this limit. Under Proposition 41, the state might not be able to exclude new special tax spending from the limit.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Auditor Costs, Mostly Paid by New Revenues. Proposition 41 would increase State Auditor costs by creating new and ongoing audit requirements. The costs would depend on (1) the number of new or increased special taxes that are proposed and approved and (2) the complexity of the programs being audited. These costs likely would be in the range of the low millions of dollars per year but would grow over time. The one-time and ongoing audit costs associated with special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature would be paid from the revenues collected by the special taxes. One-time audit costs associated with special taxes that do not ultimately appear on the ballot or are rejected by voters would be paid from the state’s General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)
Higher Costs to Print and Mail VIG. Proposition 41 would require a summary of the State Auditor’s review to appear in the VIG when a voter initiative with a special tax appears on the ballot. These audit summaries could add several pages to the VIG, which would increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative.
Possible Savings if State Auditor Recommendations Are Implemented. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to make recommendations for programs to reduce costs or improve efficiency. Proposition 41 could result in savings or improved services if policymakers implement the State Auditor’s recommendations and those recommendations prove effective. Any resulting savings would depend on future decisions and are not known.
Net Effect Not Known. The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.

ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 41
CALIFORNIANS DESERVE BETTER RESULTS FOR OUR TAX DOLLARS
Prop. 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct independent public audits of programs funded by proposed new taxes in order to increase transparency and accountability and drive better outcomes.
Californians pay some of the highest taxes in the country-on top of our high cost of living. This year alone, California’s state government will spend more than $350 billion-a 79% increase in spending since 2019. Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it.
We deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Prop. 41 requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Here’s how Prop. 41 works.
PUBLIC AUDITS TO PROVIDE ACCOUNTABILITY, TRANSPARENCY AND OVERSIGHT
Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct performance and financial audits of the programs funded by new tax measures, with the results posted publicly. The audits must:
• Track all program spending and assess whether it’s achieving its intended outcomes; • Determine whether programs have sufficient oversight and accountability; • Identify areas of waste, fraud and abuse; • Recommend how future waste and fraud can be avoided and programs made more effective.
Prop. 41 requires audits both before taxes are voted on to provide transparency to voters, and ongoing audits of programs funded by approved taxes to ensure accountability. PROP. 41: INDEPENDENT, PUBLIC INFORMATION FOR VOTERS ON PROPOSED TAXES
Before we vote on new taxes to fund programs, voters should have access to independent information about how those programs are being managed and whether they actually need more funding. Under Prop. 41, the Auditor’s findings must be posted publicly and in the Voter Information Guide-so voters can make informed decisions about new taxes without having to rely on information from special interests or politicians.
“This commonsense, long overdue reform will finally instill some transparency and accountability in state spending- ensuring Californians get better government services for the taxes we pay. It provides an independent, public report card for government spending, so government programs work better for everyone.” -Pat Fong Kushida, President/CEO of the CalAsian Chamber of Commerce
PROP. 41: A BETTER DEAL FOR TAXPAYERS
Prop. 41 doesn’t raise taxes-it protects taxpayers’ interests:
• Reduces the waste and fraud that have cost California taxpayers billions of dollars in recent years; • Requires all taxes to comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit-including its requirement that excess revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Prop. 41 ensures taxpayers get better results-not just a bigger tax bill.
“Every tax dollar we waste is a dollar that could actually help someone. Californians already pay the highest state income and sales taxes in the country-we need better transparency and accountability to make sure our tax dollars produce results. Prop. 41 delivers.” -Steve Westly, former Controller of California.

OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Prohibits any new state taxes that exclude their revenues from the state spending limit approved by voters in 1979.
For statewide special taxes, requires (1) a pre-election audit of programs that would receive funding from a voter-proposed special tax, and (2) recurring audits of programs funded by special taxes enacted after January 1, 2026.
States that other voter-approved measures appearing on the same ballot are void if they conflict with this measure and this measure receives more affirmative votes.

# Proposition 40
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires.*** Under Proposition 40, billionaires who were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to 5 percent of their net worth.
The tax would be due in 2027.
Taxpayers would have the option to spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so.
Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
***Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care.*** The state would decide how and when to spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services.
Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public.
The rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax.
Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.
#### Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 41 or 42 on this same ballot receive more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters.
This is because the courts could find that Proposition 41 or 42 conflict with Proposition 40.

November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 4
PROPOSITION 41
Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State
Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. The Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and
prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide (VIG).
Voter Initiative Process. California citizens may propose state laws and constitutional
amendments through the statewide initiative process. Supporters of an initiative collect
signatures from registered voters to qualify their initiative for the ballot. State law sets how many
valid signatures supporters must collect to qualify their initiative for the ballot. Supporters notify
the Secretary of State once they have gathered 25 percent of the necessary signatures.
Special Taxes. State taxes can be raised by the Legislature or by voters. When a “special tax”
is created, the revenue from that tax is dedicated to a specific purpose or program. For example,
certain fuel taxes can only be used to pay for public roads and other transportation programs.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and
nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments
follow the law, use money, and run their programs. These reviews are called audits. An audit
may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits
happen regularly over time while other audits are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter
Initiative Process. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would
receive funds from a new or increased special tax proposed through the voter initiative process.
This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a
measure for the ballot, which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the
ballot. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor would include in these audits, including
identifying ways to reduce an audited program’s annual costs by 10 percent. Proposition 41
requires the State Auditor to write a summary of each audit. If a proposed voter initiative with a
November 3, 2026 BallotSubject to court-ordered changes
Page 2 of 4
special tax qualifies for the ballot, Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor’s summary to be
included in the VIG. If voters approve the special tax, the cost of the one-time audit would be
paid from the new tax revenues.
Ongoing Audits of Programs Receiving Funds From New or Increased Special Taxes.
Proposition 41 also requires the State Auditor to periodically review programs that receive
funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or by voters after January 1,
2026. These ongoing audits would happen every four years. Proposition 41 specifies what the
State Auditor will include in these audits, including recommendations to improve program
efficiency. Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of this ongoing work will be paid using the new
tax revenue.
State Appropriations Limit. The State Constitution limits how much tax revenues the state
can spend each year. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes and special taxes. However,
certain types of spending, for example for infrastructure, are excluded from this limit. Under
Proposition 41, the state might not be able to exclude new special tax spending from the limit.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Auditor Costs, Mostly Paid by New Revenues. Proposition 41 would
increase State Auditor costs by creating new and ongoing audit requirements. The costs would
depend on (1) the number of new or increased special taxes that are proposed and approved and
(2) the complexity of the programs being audited. These costs likely would be in the range of the
low millions of dollars per year but would grow over time. The one-time and ongoing audit costs
associated with special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature would be paid from the
revenues collected by the special taxes. One-time audit costs associated with special taxes that do
not ultimately appear on the ballot or are rejected by voters would be paid from the state’s
General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services,
including education, health care, and prisons.)
Higher Costs to Print and Mail VIG. Proposition 41 would require a summary of the State
Auditor’s review to appear in the VIG when a voter initiative with a special tax appears on the
ballot. These audit summaries could add several pages to the VIG, which would increase state
printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative.
Possible Savings if State Auditor Recommendations Are Implemented. Proposition 41
requires the State Auditor to make recommendations for programs to reduce costs or improve
efficiency. Proposition 41 could result in savings or improved services if policymakers
implement the State Auditor’s recommendations and those recommendations prove effective.
Any resulting savings would depend on future decisions and are not known.
November 3, 2026 BallotSubject to court-ordered changes
Page 3 of 4
Net Effect Not Known. The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on
future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.
November 3, 2026 BallotSubject to court-ordered changes
Page 4 of 4
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the
California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears
on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by
special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to
exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review
government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not
change.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Unknown net fiscal effect. Increased costs for the California State Auditor to implement
new one-time and ongoing audit requirements of programs funded by special taxes.
These costs would be mostly paid from the new revenues collected from the special
taxes. Possible savings associated with implementing recommendations from the audits.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters,
the Legislature, and other policymakers.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> As the debate about taxing billionaires to fund healthcare escalates, California voters also will face decisions about whether to approve two propositions that could cancel out the proposed wealth tax.
Those measures include Proposition 41, also known as the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act.
Supporters say the measure aims to cut wasteful government spending by requiring audits for new state special taxes. It also would bar new state taxes that exempt their revenue from a state spending limit. Since this conflicts with the proposed wealth tax, opponents say it’s a “billionaire-funded smoke screen” that would block the billionaire tax.

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. The auditor would examine whether the program is achieving its goals, how to cut the program’s costs by at least 10% annually and other areas. Under the act, new or higher special taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, would be audited every four years.
The act also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit. That could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
How much they have raised
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text">
Fundraising data will be updated regularly until the election.
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The California Taxpayers Assn., the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the CalAsian Chamber of Commerce and others back the proposition. They say it would result in the government spending taxpayer dollars more wisely while improving transparency.
The bulk of the contributions to support the proposition have come from Building a Better California, data from the California secretary of state’s website show. Top contributors to Building a Better California include Sergey Brin, Google’s co-founder; John Doerr, chairman of venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins; and Eric Schmidt, the former chief executive of Google.
Advertisement
Proposition 41 “requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes,” a website for the proposition states.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the group behind the proposed billionaire tax, opposes Proposition 41.
In arguments against the measure, SEIU-UHW Chief of Staff Suzanne Jimenez wrote that the billionaires don’t care about government accountability and have been avoiding higher taxes through loopholes and tax breaks.
“This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce,” Jimenez wrote.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The proposition states its purpose is to make sure that “programs are delivering results, and that taxpayer dollars are not being lost to inefficiency, waste or abuse.” Opponents say the proposition is meant to nullify the proposed billionaire tax.

Prop 40 guide: Why ‘yes’ or ‘no’ depends on two other California propositions
By Kathleen Pender (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathleen-pender/) , Contributor Updated Oct 31, 2026 1:33 p.m.
From left, California insurance commissioner candidate Jane Kim, Sen. Bernie Sanders, independent-Vt., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., stand together onstage after the “Ballots Over Billionaires” wealth tax rally at the Curran Theatre in San Francisco.
Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle
Many Californians have strong opinions about Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the proposed “wealth tax” on billionaires. But voting for — or against — this high-stakes ballot measure in November is not as simple as voting for — or against — Prop 40.
That’s because Props 41 and 42, which never mention billionaires but are backed by some of the state’s wealthiest residents, are also on the ballot and have provisions that conflict with Prop 40. (Props 41 and 42 do not conflict with each other.)
California propositions 2026: A quick guide to help you vote (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php)
Read more : Two of California’s most powerful politicians still haven’t weighed in on Prop 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/joegarofoli/article/pelosi-harris-prop-40-california-22476930.php)
Also : Some of Prop 40’s biggest backers say it’s ‘problematic’ — but deserves voters’ support anyway (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/joegarofoli/article/prop-40-tom-steyer-22455442.php)
Related : Bernie Sanders rallies in S.F. for ‘the most important ballot initiative in the country’ (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/bernie-sanders-prop-40-billionaire-tax-22458467.php)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Under the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-10/), if two conflicting measures on the same ballot both pass with more than 50% of the vote, the one that gets the most “yes” votes prevails.
The graphic below shows the possible outcomes for which propositions could take effect, depending on how the votes come in. Voters can also use it to understand the cumulative impact of how they vote on each proposition.
What it means to vote ‘yes’ or ‘no’ on Props 40, 41 and 42
Prop 40, the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, would impose a one-time “wealth tax” on the net worth of people who were California residents as of Jan. 1, 2026 — even if they later became non-residents — and had more than $1 billion in net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. It also would exempt billionaire-tax revenues from three state-spending rules, including one known as the Gann limit.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 would conflict with Prop 40 because it would outlaw new taxes passed after Jan. 1, 2026 that are exempt from the Gann limit. Prop 42 also appears to counter Prop 40 by preventing new taxes on personal property (i.e., wealth) and taxes that apply retroactively, including those based on residency.
Backers of the billionaire tax are urging people (https://yeson40.com/) to vote “Yes” on 40 and “No” on Props 41 and 42. If voters follow that advice or, vote the exact opposite way, the outcomes would be straightforward:
If Prop 40 passes with more than 50% of the vote and Prop 41 and Prop 42 do not: The billionaire tax would take effect and the other two would not.
If Prop 40 loses and Prop 41 and/or 42 pass: The billionaire tax would fail. Prop 41 would take effect if it got a simple majority. So would Prop 42 if it passed.
But what happens if Prop 40 gets more than half the vote, and so does Prop 41 and/or 42? Here is the conventional wisdom:
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 passes with more votes than Prop 40: Prop 41 takes effect and the billionaire does not.
Prop 42 passes with more votes than Prop 40: Prop 42 takes effect, the billionaire tax dies.
Prop 40 passes with more votes than Prop 41: Prop 40 gets enacted, Prop 41 is invalidated.
Prop 40 passes with more votes than Prop 42: Prop 40 takes effect, and cancels out Prop 42.
Although these are likely scenarios, anything could happen in a court of law. The losing side could argue that its proposition doesn’t conflict with the winning one, so they should both take effect. A court would have to decide if they do conflict.
The losing side also might argue that some parts of its measure do not conflict with the winning proposition — and those parts should take effect. The California Supreme Court has rejected this piecemeal approach, but the issue could still wind up in litigation.
More importantly, any proposition declared the winner is almost sure to face legal challenges on its own merits. Anticipating such lawsuits, Prop 40 includes a procedure for “expedited judicial review of this act.”
Here’s a brief look at the measures, and how they conflict.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Signs promote “yes” on Prop 40 and “no” on Props 41 and 42 before a rally at the Curran Theatre in San Francisco in early October.
Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle Proposition 40
Under Prop 40, most billionaires would owe a one-time 5% “excise” tax on net worth above $1.1 billion. The rate would be phased in between $1 billion and $1.1 billion.
The tax would apply to publicly traded securities, private-company stock, intellectual property and physical assets such as cars and artwork.
It would exclude homes, buildings and other real estate held directly by the taxpayer, as well as most retirement accounts. One exception: Roth IRA balances above $10 million would be taxed. Physical assets located outside California would also be excluded.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The measure is sponsored by the Service Employees International Union — United Healthcare Workers West (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484470&session=2025&view=received).
The billionaire tax is what’s known as a “special tax,” in which tax revenues go toward a specific purpose rather than the state’s general fund. It stipulates that 90% of revenues would go toward Medi-Cal and other health coverage for lower-income people and the rest would go to public schools and food assistance. It’s meant to counteract the impending cuts from the Republican-led One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which was signed by President Donald Trump last year.
Prop 40 would exempt billionaire-tax revenues from constitutional requirements for education funding, budget reserves and the government-spending cap known as the Gann limit.
The Gann limit, passed by voters in 1979, restricts government spending from tax and fee revenues to 1978-79 levels, adjusted for changes in inflation and population. Anything over that limit must be refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as education.
Voters have approved many tax initiatives that exempted revenues from the Gann limit, such as the state gasoline, diesel fuel and cigarette taxes.
Proposition 41
Prop 41 has two provisions:
It would prohibit any state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026, from the Gann limit, which experts widely agree would conflict with Prop 40.
The “obvious point” of this change, “hidden deep in the Proposition 41 text, is to nullify Proposition 40,” according to a paper co-authored (https://scholarship.law.missouri.edu/facpubs/1384/) by the drafters of Prop 40. “California’s fiscal rules are so complex, the only way to do fiscal policy anymore … is to waive the existing rules,” said Brian Galle, a UC Berkeley law professor and one of the authors.
It would impose new audit requirements on programs that receive revenues from special taxes.
For any special tax initiative, meaning one placed on the ballot by citizens, the state auditor would have to conduct a detailed “preelection financial and performance audit” of programs potentially getting funds once the initiative reached 25% of required signatures. An audit summary would appear on the ballot.
For all special taxes enacted by initiative or the Legislature on or after Jan. 1, 2026, the state auditor would have to conduct a financial and performance review every four years.
These audit provisions do not conflict with Prop 40, Kaye said. He contends that if Prop 40 and 41 both pass, the audit provisions “would stand regardless of how many votes Prop 40 gets.”
Not so fast, said Darien Shanske, a UC Davis law professor and co-drafter of Prop 40. “There would be a fight about that, of course,” but he does not think those provisions would survive on their own.
Proposition 42
Prop 42, the “Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026,” would prohibit wealth taxes (on anyone, not just billionaires) and retroactive taxes. Specifically:
It would prohibit any tax enacted on or after Jan. 1, 2026, on the “ownership or control” of personal property, which includes most assets other than real estate. The ban would include taxes on savings and other financial assets — whether they are inside or outside of retirement accounts — and physical possessions. It would apply to residents regardless of their net worth.
This provision would not apply to income or capital gains from investments, which the state already taxes, nor to the taxation of real estate.
It would bar taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, that apply retroactively, including ones based on a taxpayer’s residency status.
Props 41 and 42 were created and submitted by Building a Better California (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=late1), whose major donors (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-spending-22463286.php) include Google co-founder Sergey Brin and a host of prominent CEOs, venture capitalists and other wealthy individuals. The same group is funding the opposition to Prop 40.
In their paper, the drafters of Prop 40 warn that the two competing measures “are poorly drafted in a manner that could pose serious threats to California’s fiscal future, with the potential to undermine key spending programs and potentially cause or worsen future budget crises.”
Molly Weedn, a spokesperson for Prop. 41, said via email, “Californians deserve more accountability and transparency for their hard earned tax dollars, and that is exactly what Prop 41 will offer.”
What if all three measures fail?
This is the most straightforward outcome: Nothing happens. Historically, it is also the most likely result.
Since 1912, California voters have approved 141 initiatives and rejected 256, for a success rate of 35%, according to California’s secretary of state.
Competing propositions have become “increasingly common” in recent decades, said Fredric Woocher, an attorney with Stumwasser and Woocher who specializes in election law. “It is becoming an effective technique to confuse voters and defeat measures that special interests don’t want passed.”
What does history show on conflicting props?
When voters face two conflicting ballot measures, “if they are really presented as competing alternatives, you don’t usually get them both winning,” Woocher said. “Usually you say, I will vote for one but not the other.” Or if they’re confused, they vote against both.
In November 1988, California voters faced five competing insurance measures, Props 100 through 104. Prop 103 (https://consumerwatchdog.org/insurance/insurance-reform-california-1988-insurance-wars/), sponsored by consumer groups, was the only one that got more than 50% and became law.
Legal experts believe the first time two conflicting initiatives won was in June 1988. Props 68 and 73 both dealt with campaign finance reform and got 53% and 58% of the vote, respectively. Prop 73 was declared the winner.
At first, the Fair Political Practices Commission, which was in charge of implementing the law, found a few parts of Prop 68 that did not directly conflict with Prop 73 and found them to be valid and enforceable.
But the commission was sued over that decision and in 1990, the California Supreme Court ruled against it. The court said: (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/51/744.html) “When two or more measures are competing initiatives, either because they are expressly offered as ‘all-or-nothing’ alternatives or because each creates a comprehensive regulatory scheme related to the same subject … only the provisions of the measure receiving the highest number of affirmative votes (can) be enforced.”
(Meanwhile, the key parts of Prop 73 were later invalidated on grounds unrelated to Prop 68.)
Props 40, 41 and 42 all say that if this measure receives more “yes” votes than a measure deemed to be in conflict, this measure’s provisions “shall prevail in their entirety.” Props 41 and 42 then say that “all the provisions” of the other measure “shall be null and void” while Prop 40 only says that “any conflicting provisions of the other measure or measures shall be null and void.”
Nevertheless, if two competing measures pass in November, the losing side will probably argue that all or part of it should take effect.
For example, Prop 42 spokesman Nathan Click told the Chronicle via text that “if both 40 and 42 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop 42 will not apply to the temporary (billionaire) tax, but it will apply to future taxes on personal property and personal savings.”
Galle, the co-author of Prop 40, responded that “courts will likely have to resolve some of these potential complications.”
Woocher said he thinks the courts will look at how the propositions were presented to voters. “If they are presented in the ballot arguments and campaign as ‘vote for these and not those,’ then that is significant evidence that the measure that got the most votes wins in its entirety and none of the other measures take effect.”

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem is Prop. 41 solving?
State spending is up 79% since 2019. Every year, billions of taxpayer dollars flow into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned tax money we pay to the state.
While this is a city wide example, it’s exactly the kind of reason why we need audits and transparent accountability before it’s too late to put programs back on track: Audit: San Jose failed to adequately track $300 million in homelessness spending (https://www.mercurynews.com/2024/04/13/audit-san-jose-failed-to-adequately-track-300-million-in-homelessness-spending/).
Why is this the best solution to the problem?
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by new special tax measures, with the results posted publicly in the state Voter Information Guide.
This ensures voters have detailed information about the programs they’re being asked to raise taxes to fund.
If taxes are approved, Prop. 41 also requires ongoing public audits of the programs funded by those taxes to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals and recommend improvements.
It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit — so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Why is it necessary to audit a tax proposal before it even officially qualifies for the ballot?
Providing pre-ballot information about proposed initiatives is very typical. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) and the attorney general are required by state law to provide pre-ballot information on every measure that is filed.
Prop. 41 is actually much narrower — the auditor only commences with an audit once a measure collects 25% of the signatures needed to qualify for the ballot; and it only applies to initiatives that increase taxes.
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct pre-election financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new state special taxes. The state auditor’s findings must be shared widely with the public, including in the state’s official Voter Information Guide.
This pre-election audit will give voters clear, unbiased information on the programs a proposed tax would support. These audits are more extensive than any existing information provided to voters. This fills in a critical gap in the information provided to voters. The current initiative analyses from the LAO are required by law to provide only a description of the measure. Alternatively, under Prop. 41 the auditor will also provide voters a performance evaluation of programs funded by new taxes.
If a proposed tax fails to make the ballot, the state’s general fund still has to pay for the audit. Why should taxpayers foot the bill for failed political ideas?
The value to voters in seeing this detailed information about programs before they’re asked to vote far outweighs the marginal cost of conducting the audit and printing it in the Voter Guide.
Again, this is very typical under the status quo. The LAO and the attorney general already have to provide a description and a title and summary for each and every initiative measure — including those that fail — and the General Fund pays for those costs. It is also important to recognize that the extra costs imposed on the General Fund by Prop. 41 are exceedingly small. The LAO found that Prop. 41 would impose only minimal costs upon the General Fund. Further, providing more impartial, expert information to voters when decided to approve higher taxes is money well spent.
This also fails to take into account Prop. 41’s upside. As the LAO noted in the Voter Guide, Prop. 41 would result in taxpayer savings or improved services by implementing the auditor’s recommendations.
Prop. 41 contains conflict provisions stating that if it receives more “yes” votes than a competing tax measure like Prop. 40 (the billionaire wealth tax), then Prop. 40 is nullified entirely. How do proponents respond to claims that Prop. 41 is merely a “poison pill” designed to defeat the wealth tax rather than a stand-alone oversight tool?
California has faced issues with ineffective and inefficient state spending for years: homelessness, state technology programs, EDD are just a few recent examples. Prop. 40 is just the latest proposal that would fuel ineffective spending.
Prop. 40 seeks to raise tens of billions of dollars in new tax revenue, but contains zero transparency, accountability or safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended. For instance, Prop. 40 contains no safeguards to ensure that billions of dollars don’t flow to health insurance company profits and CEOs under the guise of “saving health care.”
Prop. 40 also exempts itself from the state spending limit, so that the billions in excess tax revenues generated by the measure that would normally flow to taxpayers, schools and the state rainy day fund instead go to the Legislature with no safeguards or accountability. s like Prop. 40 can’t rip off taxpayers and schools by exempting themselves from the state spending limit.
The measure requires the state auditor to find a way to cut an audited program’s costs by 10%. Why mandate a flat 10% cut for every program, regardless of how it operates?
Prop. 41 does not in any way mandate a 10% cut for every program. What Prop. 41 actually says is that the auditor’s report should contain recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary savings of 10%. There is no mandate — this is simply one of several factors (at least 10) that the auditor must address when evaluating new spending. The point is to give voters context: For some programs a 10% budget savings may be a good idea and for others it won’t. But right now voters are totally in the dark. Exploring ways to stretch taxpayer dollars farther is always a good idea. But there is no mandate.
The sponsor of Prop. 41 is primarily backed by one billionaire. What makes Prop. 41’s billionaire backer a policy expert capable of devising smart laws for 40 million people?
Prop. 41 is supported by Build Better California, but also has a broad and diverse coalition of organizations and advocacy groups working toward a more transparent California, including small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts. Specifically, the ballot arguments in support of Prop. 41 were signed by the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the California Taxpayers Association, a former California State Auditor, the Asian Pacific Islander Chamber of Commerce and former State Controller Steve Westly.
Why should someone in favor of Prop. 40 vote for Prop. 41?
As stated above, state spending is up and billions of dollars are wasted each year in programs that, while well intended, have failed to deliver on the promises made. Prop. 41, by way of the independent State Auditor, will ensure Californians get more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes. If both Prop. 40 and Prop. 41 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop. 41’s provisions will still go into effect to the benefit of voters and taxpayers.
What is the biggest logical error opponents of Prop. 41 make?
Prop. 41’s opponents are all proponents of more taxes and more spending regardless of the accountability, oversight, transparency or trackable metrics needed to help improve the results we get for our tax dollars.
The California State Auditor’s Office is absolutely first-rate and does a fantastic job providing unbiased, nonpartisan, objective information. Getting this type of information to voters, both as part of the Voter Guide and on an ongoing basis (for taxes that are approved), is something that we should have done long ago.
What did we miss? What else should we know?
Voters support the idea of more transparency and accountability. Recent polling shows that 58% support the concept of Prop. 41:
“Q: this measure would require the independent State Auditor to conduct public performance and financial audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new taxes. Knowing this, do you support or oppose this proposal?”
